title: Custody Plea Under Guardians and Wards Act Must Go to the Court Where the Child Lives: Gujarat High Court
meta_description: Gujarat HC refuses to shift a child custody case to Rajkot, holding the Family Court where the children reside alone has jurisdiction to decide it.
case_name: XX v. YY (parties anonymised in the reports reviewed)
citation: Not available in the reports reviewed
body: A custody dispute between estranged parents turned, in the end, not on who should raise the children but on which courtroom was even entitled to decide that question. The wife had filed a custody petition under the Guardians and Wards Act before the Family Court at Himmatnagar, where the couple's children were living with their father. The husband wanted the case heard in Rajkot instead, and asked the Gujarat High Court to transfer it there.

His argument was framed as one of convenience, the kind courts hear often in matrimonial transfer petitions: a different city suited him better, for reasons that go unremarked in the reports of the order. What he was really asking for, though, was to move a custody proceeding away from the one court that had the children, and therefore the clearest view of their circumstances, within its own jurisdiction.

Justice Maulik Shelat declined. Section 9 of the Guardians and Wards Act ties jurisdiction in a custody matter to where the minor ordinarily resides, and the Court treated that link as doing real work rather than as a formality that yields to either parent's preference. A custody petition, the order holds, cannot be transferred to a family court that has no jurisdiction over the children's place of residence, however convenient that forum might be for one side. The husband's application did not even argue that the children's residence had shifted to Rajkot; it simply asked the Court to move the proceeding to a city that suited him, treating jurisdiction as a matter of party convenience rather than a statutory requirement tied to the children themselves.

That omission mattered. A transfer plea grounded in an actual change of the children's residence would have engaged Section 9 on its own terms, since the statute looks to where the minor lives now, not to where either parent happens to prefer litigating. By contrast, a transfer sought purely for the petitioning parent's convenience asks the Court to treat the statutory test as negotiable, which is precisely what Justice Maulik Shelat's order refused to do.

The reasoning behind the rule is as practical as the rule itself. A court sitting where the children actually live can call for school reports, speak to counsellors familiar with the family, and, where necessary, see the children themselves without putting either parent through the expense and disruption of travel. A court in a different city, asked to decide the same questions at a remove, loses most of that advantage and is left reconstructing the children's circumstances secondhand, relying on affidavits and transcripts rather than any direct sense of the household the children actually inhabit. Keeping the Himmatnagar Family Court in charge, on this reasoning, was not a technical point but the only arrangement that let the custody enquiry function as it was meant to.

A rule built around convenience would also create an obvious incentive problem. If a parent dissatisfied with a custody forum could simply apply to move the case to a city where they found litigation easier, the parent with the children in their physical custody would face repeated transfer applications designed less to find the right forum than to wear down the other side's resources and patience. Tying jurisdiction firmly to the children's residence closes off that route, whatever its merits might otherwise seem as a matter of litigant convenience.

The order sits alongside a line of Gujarat High Court rulings on custody and guardianship that have tried to keep Section 9's residence test from being eroded by litigants who use transfer applications, sometimes for genuine convenience and sometimes simply to inconvenience the other parent, to move a custody fight away from the forum best placed to assess the children's welfare.

For family law practitioners, the practical point is to anchor custody petitions firmly in the children's actual place of residence from the outset and to resist transfer applications on that basis rather than conceding them on convenience grounds. A client seeking to shift a custody matter to a more convenient city should expect that argument to fail unless the children's own residence has itself genuinely moved, since the Court has now made clear that the test is about where the children live, not about where either parent would rather litigate.
why_it_matters: Transfer petitions in matrimonial litigation are often used, fairly or not, to move a case to a forum more convenient for one parent, and custody disputes are no exception. This order confirms that Section 9 of the Guardians and Wards Act fixes jurisdiction to the child's actual place of residence and that a transfer application cannot be used to move a custody matter away from that forum on convenience grounds alone. Family law counsel should resist such transfer applications on jurisdictional grounds rather than argue convenience, and should expect courts to scrutinise any claimed shift in a child's residence put forward to justify a transfer.
card_summary: Gujarat HC refuses to move a custody case from Himmatnagar to Rajkot, holding that jurisdiction under the Guardians and Wards Act follows the children's actual residence, not either parent's convenience.
card_tip: Resist a transfer application in a custody matter on jurisdictional grounds by showing where the children actually reside, rather than contesting it only on convenience.
verification_notes: Both LiveLaw and Verdictum confirm the core facts: the wife's custody petition before the Family Court, Himmatnagar, where the children lived with the father, the husband's application to transfer it to Rajkot, the bench of Justice Maulik Shelat, and the holding that custody jurisdiction under the Guardians and Wards Act follows the children's place of residence and cannot be moved on convenience grounds. Verdictum reports the case under the anonymised citation 'XX v. YY', consistent with the privacy practice both outlets followed in reporting this matter, and that anonymised form is used here since no source reviewed gave the parties' actual names. Neither source stated the precise date of pronouncement; the date used here (22 October 2026) is inferred from the articles' publication timing relative to other dated Gujarat High Court reports from the same week, and falls within the batch's scope window in any event. No neutral or reported citation was located in the sources reviewed.
